title: Creation Doctrine Framework
summary: The doctrinal framework that God is the sovereign Creator of all things, giving creation order, goodness, purpose, and accountability before him.
historical_context: Creation doctrine draws from Israel's confession of the LORD as Creator amid ancient origin accounts and from later biblical texts that extend creation language to redemption and new creation.
ancient_near_east_context: Creation texts stand alongside Mesopotamian origin traditions such as Enuma Elish and Atrahasis, while Scripture presents creation as ordered by the one covenant Lord.
hebraic_worldview: Creation is good, ordered, and accountable to God; humanity receives creaturely dignity and responsibility rather than autonomous self-definition.
second_temple_context: Second Temple Jewish literature and early Christian texts often connect creation, wisdom, resurrection hope, and God's power to make all things new.
canonical_context: Creation doctrine begins the canon, grounds worship and ethics, frames Christ's cosmic significance, and culminates in new creation.
literary_context: Creation is taught through narrative, psalm, wisdom, prophecy, Gospel, epistle, and apocalyptic vision rather than a single doctrinal passage alone.
covenantal_significance: Creation grounds covenant because the Creator has authority to bless, command, judge, redeem, and renew his world.
original_audience: Readers learning Scripture's account of God, world, and human vocation
historical_setting: Canonical teaching from Genesis through Revelation
canonical_role: Foundational doctrine for God, humanity, worship, ethics, providence, redemption, and new creation.
canonical_placement: Foundational doctrine introduced in Genesis and developed across the canon
intertextuality: Genesis 1-2 grounds later worship and wisdom texts.
John 1 and Colossians 1 connect creation to Christ.
Revelation 21-22 completes creation doctrine in new creation.
timeline: Wisdom and worship confess the Creator
Christ revealed as agent and heir of creation

scripture_references.notes: God creates and declares creation good

interpretive_notes.note: Creation doctrine should hold together God, world, humanity, worship, ethics, and new creation instead of narrowing to origin mechanics only.
The New Testament's Christological creation texts develop, rather than replace, the Old Testament confession of the Creator.

common_questions: What is the doctrine of creation?
Why does creation matter for biblical theology?
How does creation connect to new creation?

hermeneutical_lens.immediate_literary_context: Creation texts should be read according to their genre, whether narrative, hymn, wisdom, Gospel, epistle, or apocalypse.
hermeneutical_lens.book_context: Genesis establishes the foundation, while later books use creation to teach worship, wisdom, Christology, and hope.
hermeneutical_lens.canonical_context: Creation begins and new creation completes the canon's world-oriented scope.
hermeneutical_lens.covenant_context: The Creator's authority grounds covenant blessing, command, judgment, and renewal.
hermeneutical_lens.historical_context: Israel's confession of the Creator stands amid ancient origin traditions.
hermeneutical_lens.ancient_near_east_context: Ancient origin stories supply comparison, but biblical creation theology has its own monotheistic shape.
hermeneutical_lens.second_temple_jewish_context: Creation, wisdom, resurrection, and renewal are often held together in later Jewish and Christian reflection.
hermeneutical_lens.original_audience: God's people confessing the Creator in worship and obedience.
hermeneutical_lens.genre: Doctrine synthesized from narrative, poetry, wisdom, Gospel, epistle, and apocalypse.
hermeneutical_lens.messianic_christological_trajectory: Christ is revealed as the one through whom and for whom all things exist.
hermeneutical_lens.christological_significance: Creation doctrine is deepened by New Testament claims about Christ's role in creation and reconciliation.
